title: Power-Performance Scaling
summary: Why Dennard scaling broke down, and how DVFS manages the power budget that resulted.

slides.subTitle: The historical assumption
slides.markdown:
**Dennard scaling** (1970s observation) held that as transistors shrink, their voltage and current shrink proportionally too — so power *density* (power per unit area) stays roughly constant even as you pack in more, faster transistors. That meant each new process generation could deliver higher clock speeds **for free**, power-wise.

For decades this was the engine behind steadily rising clock speeds: smaller transistors just kept getting faster without the chip getting proportionally hotter.

slides.subTitle: Leakage stopped shrinking
slides.markdown:
Dennard's assumption depended on voltage scaling down as fast as transistor size did. But past a certain point (roughly the mid-2000s), voltage couldn't keep shrinking — going lower made transistors leak too much current even when "off" (static/leakage power, previous topic), and made switching unreliable.

Once voltage scaling stalled while transistor density kept improving, power density started **rising** with each new generation instead of staying flat — the free lunch of ever-higher clock speeds ended.

slides.subTitle: Clock speed, power, and core count over time
slides.markdown:
Plotting three trends together shows the pivot clearly.

![A timeline of clock speed, power, and core count showing the post-Dennard inflection point](assets/dennard-inflection-timeline.svg)

Clock speed climbed steeply for decades, then flattened hard right around the point power density stopped cooperating — and core count picked up almost exactly where clock speed leveled off.

assets.alt: A timeline of clock speed, power, and core count showing the post-Dennard inflection point

slides.subTitle: Multicore instead of faster cores
slides.markdown:
Once single-core clock speed hit its power wall, the industry's main lever for using ever-more-plentiful transistors shifted to **adding more cores** rather than making one core faster (cross-link: multicore-motivation-and-smp). More cores can raise total throughput within roughly the same power envelope, as long as software can actually use them in parallel — which is exactly the condition Amdahl's Law puts a limit on.

This is the direct historical link between a power constraint (Dennard's breakdown) and an architectural one (the shift to parallelism) — one caused the other.

slides.subTitle: Trading performance for power at runtime
slides.markdown:
**Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS)** lets a chip lower its voltage and clock frequency together during low-demand periods (idle, light load), then raise them again when heavier work arrives — trading some latency for a large power saving when full performance isn't needed.

This is the runtime answer to the same voltage-squared lever from the power-and-energy topic: since a chip rarely needs peak performance every single moment, DVFS captures large average power savings without giving up peak capability when it's actually demanded.

slides.subTitle: Race to idle vs sustained low power
slides.markdown:
| Strategy | Approach | Wins when |
|---|---|---|
| Race to idle | Run at high voltage/frequency to finish the task fast, then drop to a very low-power idle state | Idle power is much lower than active power, so finishing fast and sleeping beats a slow, steady pace |
| Sustained lower power | Run the whole task at reduced voltage/frequency throughout | Idle power isn't much lower than active power, or the task can't tolerate the burst of heat/noise from running fast |

**How to decide:** race-to-idle tends to win on mobile/battery devices where deep sleep states draw very little power, so total energy favors sprinting then resting. Sustained lower power suits systems where thermal or power-delivery limits make a sudden burst of high power impractical, even briefly.

slides.subTitle: "Just clock it higher"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If I need more performance, the CPU can always just run at a higher clock speed."

**Why it's wrong:** modern CPUs are **power- and thermal-limited**. "Turbo boost" runs briefly at a higher clock, but only until the thermal or power budget is hit — then the clock is forced back down (throttling) regardless of the workload. There's no free, sustained higher clock sitting unused.

**Correct model:** peak clock is a burst capability bounded by power/thermal budget, not a dial left turned up. Sustained performance follows the trade-offs covered in this topic.

slides.subTitle: When you have more transistors than you can afford to power on
slides.markdown:
Post-Dennard, transistor count kept growing (Moore's Law didn't stop) but the power budget per unit area did not — meaning a chip can now fit more functional units than it could ever run **simultaneously** at full power without overheating. This gap between transistors you *have* and transistors you can *afford to power on at once* is called **dark silicon**.

In practice, this is exactly why modern high-end chips ship packed with specialized units that sit idle most of the time — a video decode block, a neural accelerator, extra cache — rather than more general-purpose cores running simultaneously: powering on everything at once would exceed the thermal budget, so the design bets that different workloads light up different subsets of the chip at different times. Dark silicon is a direct, unavoidable consequence of the same power wall that ended Dennard scaling and pushed the industry toward heterogeneous, specialized silicon instead of just adding more identical general-purpose cores.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: the power budget behind a core-count decision
slides.subTitle: Why doubling cores doesn't double a chip's power draw
slides.markdown:
A chip's power budget is fixed at 150W. Each core at full clock draws roughly 15W; base/uncore (memory controller, shared cache, I/O) draws a fixed 30W regardless of core count.

```
available power for cores = 150W - 30W = 120W
max cores at full clock simultaneously = 120W / 15W = 8 cores

if the design ships 16 cores (more than the power budget supports at full clock):
  running all 16 at once requires clocking each down so total stays <= 120W
  120W / 16 cores = 7.5W/core -- roughly half the full-clock power per core
  lower power per core (via DVFS) means each core also runs at a lower clock
```

This is exactly why many-core chips throttle per-core clock speed down as more cores become active under load — the power budget, not the transistor count, is the real ceiling, and a chip with "16 cores" often can't actually run all 16 at their rated peak clock simultaneously without exceeding its thermal design power.
